The patient will need to continue going to dialysis three times a week.

The patient died from multiple complications including acute hypoxemic respiratory failure, gastrointestinal hemorrhage with ischemic colitis, and acute on chronic kidney injury. He received continuous veno-venous hemodialysis for volume overload due to left heart failure and steroid therapy. The GI bleed recurred after tracheostomy; he was found to be a poor operative candidate. Given grim prognosis, he was made comfort measures only and aggressive treatments including transfusions were discontinued.

The bleeding was caused by an upper gastrointestinal bleed from esophageal varices. The patient underwent emergent endoscopy with banding in the ICU. He was resuscitated with blood products including 4 packed red blood cells, 2 platelets, and 1 fresh frozen plasma. He was treated with IV proton pump inhibitor and octreotide drip for 48 hours, plus 5 days of IV ceftriaxone. The bleeding also caused hypotension and demand ischemia.

During hospitalization, the patient had ventricular tachycardia, a life-threatening heart rhythm. The patient was discharged with a lifevest, worn externally, which will shock the patient if this dangerous rhythm occurs again. The patient was also started on Metoprolol succinate to lower heart rate and blood pressure.

The patient awoke neurologically intact post-operatively but experienced postoperative confusion and agitation treated with Haldol and Zyprexa. He remained in the CVICU until his mental status improved. Psychiatry and social work were consulted to evaluate postoperative confusion with hallucinations. His mental status returned to baseline by postoperative day 9, when he was cleared for discharge to home with visiting nurse services.

The patient has anoxic brain injury after a PEA arrest during VT ablation, resulting in mild to moderate encephalopathy with stable reduction in gray-white differentiation on CT head. EEG showed no epileptiform discharges or electrographic seizures. He has a tracheostomy and ventilator, PEG tube for feeding, and is non-verbal at baseline. After completing a week of antibiotics, she remained persistently febrile, and all culture data was negative. Antibiotics were then held. The patient is currently being treated with multi-drug therapy for presumed pleural tuberculosis.

The patient's intracerebral hemorrhage was treated conservatively with blood pressure control and monitoring. He was offered a Factor VII trial but refused, and there were no other alternative therapies indicated. He was monitored in the neuro ICU with blood pressure initially controlled using labetalol infusion for goal systolic blood pressure less than 140. Aspirin and heparin products were held given the hemorrhage. Repeat imaging showed the hemorrhage was stable.

The patient's acute renal failure likely started before presentation from poor forward flow from initial cardiogenic failure and was probably exacerbated by 320 ccs of contrast received in the cath lab. She developed muddy brown casts on urine analysis. Due to hyperkalemia to 6.8 and anuria immediately post catheterization, she was treated with CVVHD for volume overload and hyperkalemia. She failed repeated trials off of CRRT and is likely now dialysis-dependent.

The patient underwent exploratory laparotomy for necrotic uterus with abscess, then required second surgery for perforated diverticulitis with pelvic peritonitis requiring colon resection and colostomy placement. She developed polymicrobial sepsis with bacteremia. At discharge, she was slowly getting better with stable vital signs, decreasing white blood cell count, and was afebrile. She required intravenous antibiotics, VAC dressing for wound healing, and rehabilitation for continued recovery.

The patient's pain was well controlled with Percocet (oxycodone-acetaminophen 5-325 mg). She was discharged on 1-2 tablets every 4-6 hours as needed for pain, to be taken with food. She was also prescribed acetaminophen 325 mg, two tablets every 4-6 hours as needed. The discharge instructions specified not to take Percocet with Ativan (lorazepam) concurrently.

The patient's gum bleeding is caused by thrombocytopenia related to multiple factors: end-stage liver disease (ESLD), splenomegaly (19.3 cm), critical illness, and multiple antibiotics that are reversibly myelosuppressive. The bleeding diathesis is related more to the low platelet count (as low as 45K when bleeding occurred) than to elevated INR. Aminocaproic acid was used for gum bleeding treatment. There is no mention of oral cancer concerns in the medical record.
